questions.question: What is Spring Boot Actuator and how do you secure its endpoints in production?
questions.title: Spring Boot Actuator — Endpoints and Security
questions.direct_answer: Spring Boot Actuator exposes operational HTTP and JMX endpoints — `/health`, `/info`, `/metrics`, `/env`, `/beans`, `/heapdump`, `/threaddump` — without writing custom monitoring code. By default only **`/health` and `/info` are exposed over HTTP**; everything else requires explicit opt-in via `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include`. In production, layer four defenses: **expose only what monitoring needs**, **secure with Spring Security role-based access**, **isolate on a separate `management.server.port`**, and **split health into liveness/readiness groups** for Kubernetes probes. Setting `exposure.include=*` in production is the most common Actuator security incident.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you know Actuator endpoints are a security risk if left open and can describe a layered defence strategy
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Exposing `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*` in production without authentication, leaking environment variables, heap dumps, and internal metrics
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Describe using a separate `management.server.port` with a firewall rule so only internal services reach Actuator, plus `/actuator/health` groups for liveness and readiness probes in Kubernetes

sections.title: Production Observability — and a Security Liability If Left Open
sections.content:
Spring Boot Actuator adds **production-ready endpoints** that give instant visibility into a running application: health checks, metrics, environment inspection, thread dumps, heap dumps, bean graphs. No custom monitoring code, no extra agent — add the starter, configure exposure, and you have observability.

The danger is that several endpoints leak **dangerously sensitive information**.
- `/env` shows every environment variable, including database passwords and API keys.
- `/heapdump` lets anyone download a full JVM snapshot containing in-memory secrets and session tokens.
- `/beans` reveals the entire architecture.
- Setting `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=*` in production — recommended in many tutorials for development — is the most common Actuator security mistake.

**The default in Spring Boot 2.x+ is conservative**: only `/health` and `/info` are exposed over HTTP. Everything else requires explicit opt-in. Production hardening is a layered strategy of exposure control, authentication, network isolation, and health-group design — not just one property change.

sections.title: Actuator Endpoint Exposure Pipeline
sections.content:
```mermaid
flowchart TB
    Request["HTTP request to /actuator/*"]
    PortCheck{"On management.server.port?"}
    Filter["Endpoint exposure filter"]
    Include["management.endpoints.web.exposure.include"]
    Exclude["management.endpoints.web.exposure.exclude"]
    Enabled{"Endpoint enabled?"}
    Security["Spring Security filter chain"]
    Allow["EndpointRequest matcher"]
    Health["/health  /info  permitAll"]
    Other["all other endpoints  hasRole ACTUATOR"]
    Handler["Endpoint handler"]
    Reject["404 Not Found"]
    Forbid["401 / 403"]

    Request --> PortCheck
    PortCheck -->|yes| Filter
    PortCheck -->|wrong port| Reject
    Filter --> Include
    Include --> Exclude
    Exclude --> Enabled
    Enabled -->|no| Reject
    Enabled -->|yes| Security
    Security --> Allow
    Allow --> Health
    Allow --> Other
    Health --> Handler
    Other -->|authorized| Handler
    Other -->|not authorized| Forbid
```

sections.title: Layer 1 — Exposure Control
sections.content:
**Default exposure**
- Spring Boot 2.x+ exposes only `/health` and `/info` over HTTP
- All other endpoints (`/env`, `/beans`, `/heapdump`, `/threaddump`) are off by default
- JMX exposure is broader but JMX is rarely exposed externally

**Production exposure list**
- Limit to what monitoring genuinely needs: `health`, `metrics`, `info`, `prometheus`
- Never set `include=*` outside of local development
- Use `exclude` to subtract specific endpoints if a starter forced one on

**Configuration**

```properties
management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics,prometheus
management.endpoints.web.exposure.exclude=env,beans,heapdump,threaddump
management.endpoint.health.show-details=when-authorized
management.endpoint.health.show-components=when-authorized
```

**Health detail levels**
- `never` — only `UP`/`DOWN` (safe for public load balancer checks)
- `when-authorized` — authenticated callers see component-level details
- `always` — leaks DB connection strings; never use in production

sections.title: Layer 2 — Spring Security on Actuator
sections.content:
**Why a dedicated filter chain**
- Actuator endpoints should not share rules with the main API
- Mixing them risks accidental exposure when application security changes
- `EndpointRequest` matcher targets only Actuator paths so the rule is scoped

**A typical secure configuration**
- `/health` and `/info` stay public for load-balancer probes
- All other Actuator endpoints require an `ACTUATOR` role
- HTTP Basic auth is enough for an internal monitoring user

```java
@Bean
public SecurityFilterChain actuatorSecurity(HttpSecurity http) throws Exception {
    return http
        .securityMatcher(EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint())
        .authorizeHttpRequests(auth -> auth
            .requestMatchers(EndpointRequest.to("health", "info")).permitAll()
            .anyRequest().hasRole("ACTUATOR")
        )
        .httpBasic(Customizer.withDefaults())
        .csrf(csrf -> csrf.disable())
        .build();
}
```

**Operational notes**
- The `securityMatcher(EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint())` ensures this chain only handles `/actuator/**`
- A second `SecurityFilterChain` bean handles application endpoints separately
- Disable CSRF on Actuator only — POST endpoints like `/loggers` need it off for tooling integration

sections.title: Layer 3 — Network Isolation via Separate Management Port
sections.content:
**The strongest defence is not authentication**
- Setting `management.server.port` moves all Actuator endpoints to a separate TCP port
- The application port (8080) is exposed publicly through the ingress
- The management port (9090) is reachable only from internal networks

**Configuration**

```properties
server.port=8080
management.server.port=9090
management.server.address=10.0.0.0
management.endpoints.web.base-path=/actuator
management.server.ssl.enabled=true
management.server.ssl.client-auth=need
```

**Operational benefits**
- `/heapdump`, `/env`, `/threaddump` are unreachable from the internet regardless of auth config
- Even a security misconfig cannot leak data because port 9090 is not routed externally
- `management.server.address=127.0.0.1` binds to localhost only on single-server deployments
- The management port supports independent SSL — mutual TLS for internal monitoring
- In Kubernetes, a NetworkPolicy restricts port 9090 to the monitoring namespace

sections.title: Layer 4 — Health Groups for Kubernetes Liveness and Readiness
sections.content:
**Why one /health is not enough**
- Liveness probe asks: is this process alive and not deadlocked?
- Readiness probe asks: can this pod serve traffic right now?
- Mixing them causes pod restarts when only routing changes are needed

**The classic mistake**
- Including a database health check in the liveness probe
- Database goes down → every pod fails liveness → Kubernetes restarts every pod
- Restarts do nothing useful because the database is still down
- Outcome: cascading restart storm during a downstream incident

**Spring Boot health groups**

```properties
management.endpoint.health.group.liveness.include=ping
management.endpoint.health.group.readiness.include=db,redis,kafka
management.endpoint.health.probes.enabled=true
```

**Endpoint mapping**
- `/actuator/health/liveness` — minimal check; pod restart only on real process failure
- `/actuator/health/readiness` — full dependency check; pod removed from service when DOWN
- Auto-enabled in Kubernetes (detected via `KUBERNETES_SERVICE_HOST` env var)
- Wire into pod spec `livenessProbe` and `readinessProbe` independently

sections.title: Configuration Trade-offs
sections.content:
**When `show-details=always` helps:**
- Internal-only deployments behind a corporate VPN with no external exposure
- Local development where component-level health is the point
- Diagnostic environments where debugging speed matters more than security

**When `show-details=always` hurts:**
- Any production endpoint reachable from the internet
- Health endpoint included in load balancer probes that bypass auth
- Multi-tenant environments where component names leak architecture

**Watch for:**
- Custom `HealthIndicator` beans that include user-supplied data in `Health.down().withDetail(...)` — leaks PII
- `/loggers` POST endpoint that lets anyone change log levels at runtime; protect with role
- Spring Boot defaulting `/info` content from `git.properties` — leaks commit hash and build time

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`exposure.include=*` is a production incident waiting to happen** — `/env` dumps passwords; `/heapdump` gives the full JVM heap; expose only `health,info,metrics,prometheus`.
- **Separate `management.server.port`** — isolates Actuator from the app port; combine with NetworkPolicy or firewall to restrict to internal networks.
- **`/actuator/health` shows `UP`/`DOWN` only by default** — `show-details=when-authorized` reveals component-level info to authenticated users only.
- **`EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint()`** — the `securityMatcher` that scopes a `SecurityFilterChain` to Actuator routes; keeps Actuator security separate from app security.
- **Health groups split liveness from readiness** — DB checks belong in readiness only; mixing them causes Kubernetes restart storms during downstream outages.
- **Custom `HealthIndicator` for app-specific checks** — implement the interface, return `Health.up()` / `Health.down().withDetail(...)`; gets included automatically.
- **`/actuator/prometheus` exposes Micrometer metrics** — add `micrometer-registry-prometheus`; no code changes; Prometheus scrapes the endpoint.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Boot Actuator gives you production observability — health, metrics, environment, thread dumps — without deploying a separate monitoring agent. The defaults are safe for development; exposing it fully in production is a security incident.

**The four hardening layers**
- Exposure control: `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include=health,info,metrics,prometheus` — never `*`
- Spring Security with `EndpointRequest.toAnyEndpoint()` — keep `/health` and `/info` public, require `ACTUATOR` role for everything else
- Separate management port: `management.server.port=9090` — moves Actuator off the public port; combine with a NetworkPolicy so only monitoring can reach it
- Health groups: split `liveness` (minimal ping) from `readiness` (DB, Redis, Kafka) so Kubernetes restarts only when the process is genuinely broken

**Why exposure matters**
- `/env` leaks every property including passwords if injected as env vars
- `/heapdump` returns the full JVM memory — secrets, session tokens, decrypted credentials
- `/beans` and `/conditions` reveal the architecture and let attackers plan further probes

**Health detail control**
- `management.endpoint.health.show-details=when-authorized` — `UP`/`DOWN` for the load balancer, component details for authenticated callers
- Custom `HealthIndicator` beans add app-specific checks — external API reachability, queue depth — and integrate into the same response monitoring already watches

In an interview, I'd emphasize that **the strongest defence is network isolation**, not authentication. Authentication is a layer; an isolated management port behind a NetworkPolicy is a moat.

questions.question: How do you build a custom Actuator endpoint and expose Micrometer metrics to Prometheus?
questions.title: Custom Actuator Endpoint and Prometheus Exposition
questions.direct_answer: Create a custom Actuator endpoint with `@Endpoint(id = "name")` and methods annotated `@ReadOperation`, `@WriteOperation`, or `@DeleteOperation` — Spring Boot exposes them at `/actuator/name` automatically. Register the bean and add the ID to `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include`. For Prometheus, add `micrometer-registry-prometheus` and Spring Boot auto-configures `/actuator/prometheus` returning OpenMetrics-format text. Inject `MeterRegistry` to publish custom metrics: counters, gauges, timers, distribution summaries. Always tag metrics with **bounded label sets** — high-cardinality tags (user IDs, request IDs) explode Prometheus storage and become operationally unmanageable.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether you can implement custom Actuator extension points and integrate Spring Boot metrics into a Prometheus monitoring pipeline
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Tagging metrics with unbounded values (user IDs, URL paths with IDs), causing Prometheus cardinality explosion and OOM in the time-series database
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention `MeterFilter` for cardinality limits, `@Timed` annotation for declarative timer instrumentation, and the difference between Counter/Gauge/Timer/DistributionSummary metric types

sections.title: Custom Endpoints and Metrics — Two Different Extension Points
sections.content:
Spring Boot Actuator supports two extension paths that solve different problems.
- **Custom endpoints** (`@Endpoint`) expose application-specific operational data through the same `/actuator/*` URL space — feature flag state, internal queue depth, license expiry, deploy metadata.
- They behave like first-class Actuator endpoints: the same exposure controls, the same security configuration.

**Custom metrics** publish through Micrometer's `MeterRegistry`.
- Counters track event counts, gauges read instantaneous values, timers measure latency distributions.
- Spring Boot wires Micrometer to a registry implementation based on what's on the classpath — Prometheus, Datadog, CloudWatch, Graphite.
- Adding `micrometer-registry-prometheus` makes Spring Boot auto-configure `/actuator/prometheus` returning **OpenMetrics-format** text that Prometheus scrapes.

**The trap is cardinality**.
- A `Counter` tagged with user ID looks innocent in development but creates one time series per user in production — millions of series in Prometheus, gigabytes of memory, and metrics queries that time out.
- Tag design is the single most important decision when adding custom metrics.

sections.title: Building a Custom @Endpoint
Publishing Custom Metrics with MeterRegistry
Prometheus Exposition and Tag Cardinality
sections.content:
**Add the registry**
- Add `io.micrometer:micrometer-registry-prometheus` to dependencies
- Spring Boot auto-configures `/actuator/prometheus`
- Add `prometheus` to `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include`

**Endpoint output**

```
# HELP orders_placed_total Total orders successfully placed
# TYPE orders_placed_total counter
orders_placed_total{region="us-east-1",} 4823.0

# HELP orders_db_save_seconds  
# TYPE orders_db_save_seconds summary
orders_db_save_seconds{quantile="0.5",} 0.012
orders_db_save_seconds{quantile="0.95",} 0.048
orders_db_save_seconds{quantile="0.99",} 0.183
```

**Cardinality rules**
- Tag values must come from a **bounded set** — region, status code, HTTP method, error class
- Never tag with user ID, request ID, full URL path, customer ID, or any unbounded value
- One unbounded tag turns one metric into millions of series — Prometheus OOM
- Total series target: under 100,000 per app instance for healthy operation

**Enforce limits with MeterFilter**

```java
@Bean
MeterFilter cardinalityLimit() {
    return MeterFilter.maximumAllowableTags(
        "http.server.requests", "uri", 100,
        MeterFilter.deny()
    );
}
```

**Prometheus scrape configuration** (on the Prometheus side)

```yaml
scrape_configs:
  - job_name: 'spring-boot-app'
    metrics_path: '/actuator/prometheus'
    scrape_interval: 15s
    static_configs:
      - targets: ['app:8080']
```

sections.title: Micrometer Meter Types and When to Use Each
sections.content:
Choose the meter type that matches the question you want to answer at query time, not the data shape during collection.

| Meter | Captures | Example | Prometheus Output |
|---|---|---|---|
| `Counter` | Monotonic event count | Orders placed, errors thrown | `_total` suffix; use `rate()` to get per-second |
| `Gauge` | Instantaneous value | Queue depth, cache size, active connections | Single sample; use `_size` or `_count` naming |
| `Timer` | Latency distribution + count | Method execution time, DB query latency | `_seconds` summary with quantiles |
| `DistributionSummary` | Non-time value distribution | Response payload size, batch size | `_bytes` or `_count` summary with quantiles |
| `LongTaskTimer` | Long-running task duration | Active background jobs, scheduled task durations | `_active_seconds` for in-flight measurement |

**The naming convention** matters for Prometheus tooling: use `_total` for counters, `_seconds` for time durations, `_bytes` for sizes. Micrometer applies these suffixes automatically when exporting to Prometheus, but the base name should follow the convention so dashboards and alerts work.

sections.title: Custom Metrics Design Trade-offs
sections.content:
**When custom metrics help:**
- Business KPIs not exposed by framework metrics — orders per second, revenue, signups
- Per-feature observability — feature flag adoption, A/B test split
- Domain-specific SLOs — checkout latency, payment success rate

**When custom metrics hurt:**
- Logging implemented as metrics — every event tagged with unbounded values
- Duplicating framework metrics — Spring Boot already publishes HTTP, JVM, JDBC pools
- Metrics for low-frequency events better tracked as logs or traces

**Watch for:**
- High cardinality from URL path tags — use `MeterFilter` to bucket or drop
- Counter resets on app restart — use `rate()` in PromQL, never raw counter values
- Gauge values from expensive computation — Micrometer calls the supplier on every scrape
- Tag drift across app versions — adding/removing tags creates inconsistent dashboards

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Endpoint(id = "...")`** — registers a custom Actuator endpoint at `/actuator/{id}`; combine with `@ReadOperation`/`@WriteOperation`/`@DeleteOperation` and `@Selector` for path variables.
- **Custom endpoints respect exposure rules** — must add the ID to `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include`; Spring Security `EndpointRequest` matchers apply automatically.
- **`MeterRegistry` is the central metric API** — Spring Boot auto-configures it based on classpath; add `micrometer-registry-prometheus` for Prometheus exposition.
- **`/actuator/prometheus` returns OpenMetrics text** — Prometheus scrapes it; no app code changes beyond the dependency and exposure include.
- **Cardinality kills Prometheus** — never tag with unbounded values (user ID, URL with IDs); use `MeterFilter.maximumAllowableTags` to enforce limits.
- **`@Timed` annotation for declarative timers** — requires a `TimedAspect` bean; cleaner than manual `Timer.record()` for service methods.
- **Meter type drives query semantics** — Counter → `rate()`; Gauge → instantaneous; Timer → `_seconds_bucket` for percentile queries.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring Boot Actuator has two extension points: **custom endpoints** for app-specific operational data and **custom metrics** through Micrometer for everything that's quantitative.

**Custom endpoints**
- Annotate a Spring bean with `@Endpoint(id = "features")`
- Add `@ReadOperation`, `@WriteOperation`, `@DeleteOperation` methods
- `@Selector` captures path variables: `/actuator/features/{name}`
- Register by adding the ID to `management.endpoints.web.exposure.include`
- Same Spring Security rules apply as built-in endpoints

**Custom metrics**
- Inject `MeterRegistry`; create `Counter`, `Gauge`, `Timer`, or `DistributionSummary`
- Use `@Timed` for declarative method timing — needs a `TimedAspect` bean
- Add `micrometer-registry-prometheus` and Spring Boot auto-configures `/actuator/prometheus`
- Output is OpenMetrics text; Prometheus scrapes it on a configured interval

**Cardinality is the trap**
- Never tag metrics with unbounded values: user ID, request ID, URL path with IDs
- A `Counter` tagged with user ID becomes one time series per user — millions of series, Prometheus OOM
- Use `MeterFilter.maximumAllowableTags` to cap tag cardinality
- Bounded tags are fine: region, HTTP method, status code, error class

In an interview, I'd close with the operational rule: **measure first, instrument second**. Spring Boot already publishes HTTP latency, JVM memory, JDBC pool stats, and Tomcat thread counts through Micrometer — no custom code needed. Add custom metrics only for KPIs the framework doesn't already cover.
